C-01.1.answer: A write with no content and a shell call with no text have nothing to scan, so there is no secret to leak and the call goes on to the ordinary rules; but a scan that cannot run (an error inside the scanner) is a deny, never a quiet pass. A secret found is always a deny; absence of a secret is the only way past this step.
C-01.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::writing ordinary content and running an ordinary command are allowed

C-01.2.answer: The tests write content without a secret and run a plain command (allowed), then write the same content with a secret and run a command carrying one (denied), so removing the secret is the only difference between pass and deny — the check is not optional.
C-01.2.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::an Edit or Write whose content is a secret is denied

C-02.1.answer: The rules are the existing scanner's set (src/secret-scan.mjs RULES), applied through one scanText to every secret surface; nothing is hand-listed per call site. The gitleaks 222-rule expansion needs the upstream file fetched at a pinned commit (a download) and is deferred to the owner's go — the spec says so and the hook already runs every rule scanText carries.
C-02.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::an Edit or Write whose content is a secret is denied

C-02.2.answer: The same scan runs on all three secret surfaces — a write's content, a shell command's text, and an apply_patch body — and for every agent (claude-code, cursor, codex) through the one evaluate path, so the rule 'a secret written, printed or read is denied' is applied once and everywhere.
C-02.2.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a shell command that prints a literal secret is denied

C-03.1.answer: Each secret deny has a test with the bug put back: removing the content scan makes the write-secret and print-secret tests go red, and a fiction-token exemption still passes an ordinary write, so the check fails for the reason it names and only that.
C-03.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::an Edit or Write whose content is a secret is denied

C-03.2.answer: The tests drive the real hook (normalize + evaluate) with a real Write/Edit payload and a real Bash payload, observing the deny the agent would read, not a function return in isolation.
C-03.2.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a shell command that prints a literal secret is denied

C-03.3.answer: The deny is tied to a real scanText match on the real content, not to a flag: the test asserts the deny carries the matched rule id, and the control write (no secret) passes, so the check fails only when a secret is actually present.
C-03.3.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a secret block names its rule and fingerprint, never the value

C-04.1.answer: The scanned content and command text are bounded by the hook's MAX_PAYLOAD (1 MiB whole payload) and the scanner's own MAX_SCAN_BYTES and per-line cap; the rules are linear, non-backtracking, run without the u flag on capped input — a refusal/size bound, never a stopwatch.
C-04.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::an Edit or Write whose content is a secret is denied

C-05.1.answer: Each sentence the spec adds for the hook (a written secret denied, a printed secret denied, a read secret denied, the decision line carries the rule and fingerprint not the value) has a test that fails without it; the deferred 222-rule port is marked as needing the fetch, not claimed done.
C-05.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a secret block names its rule and fingerprint, never the value

C-05.2.answer: The deny reason names the rule and the keyed fingerprint a person can match against sakk scan, and never prints the secret value; the decision-log line carries the same, so what the tool reports is actable without leaking the secret.
C-05.2.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a secret block names its rule and fingerprint, never the value

C-07.1.answer: The write content, command text and patch body are agent-written: they are scanned, never executed, and only a keyed fingerprint (not the value) leaves the scanner into the reason or the log; the inputs are size-bounded before scanning.
C-07.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a secret block names its rule and fingerprint, never the value

C-07.2.answer: The agent cannot clear a secret block: it is a deny the agent reads, not something it can settle or approve; a person removes the secret from the content or command. Writing the guard's own config stays denied too.
C-07.2.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::an Edit or Write whose content is a secret is denied

C-08.1.answer: Secret detection is on the content and the command text, not the path, so a path alias does not change the verdict; the file path itself is still canonicalized for the existing secret.read rule, one name only.
C-08.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a shell command that prints a literal secret is denied

C-09.1.answer: The check runs on the states a real call reaches: a Write, an Edit (new text), a MultiEdit, an apply_patch body, and a Bash command — each exercised; a tool with no content surface (Read, Grep) is unaffected and still judged by the read rules.
C-09.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a shell command that prints a literal secret is denied

revisions.answer: The original answer named MultiEdit, NotebookEdit and apply_patch as exercised, but the tests drove only Write/Edit/Bash — the review (F-160) caught the overclaim. Now each write surface (Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit), the apply_patch body and the Bash command has a named test, and a command that tokenizes to zero actions still denies on a call-level floor.
revisions.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a secret written through MultiEdit or NotebookEdit is denied, not only Write/Edit

C-09.2.answer: It fires inside the installed hook's evaluate (the path a real call takes), for claude-code, cursor and codex, shown by tests that drive evaluate — not only configured.
C-09.2.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::an Edit or Write whose content is a secret is denied

revisions.answer: The original answer claimed all three agents fired through evaluate, but only claude-code was driven by a test and cursor captured content only for Write (F-160). Now codex (apply_patch) and cursor (every write surface, not only Write) each have a test that drives evaluate to a deny.
revisions.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a cursor Edit (not just cursor Write) whose new content is a secret is denied

C-10.1.answer: The secret scan is a step in evaluate, not a rule in a doc; a test fails if the write-content or command-text scan is removed, so the step cannot be quietly dropped.
C-10.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::an Edit or Write whose content is a secret is denied

C-10.2.answer: Every write and shell route (Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit, apply_patch, Bash) goes through the one evaluate scan, and the content it scans is the content of the call it is judging — there is no second route that writes content the scan did not see.
C-10.2.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a shell command that prints a literal secret is denied

C-12.1.answer: A match is judged with the existing scanner's context handling (F-11/F-63): a declared fiction token anywhere in or swallowed by a match does not exempt a real secret beside it; the hook reuses scanText, so that context rule applies unchanged.
C-12.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a fiction token does not exempt a real secret beside it

C-13.1.answer: The eight existing rules the hook runs are measured both-sided in the scanner's tests (true samples caught, benign inputs left alone); the full gitleaks both-sided corpus (the C-13 stopline, due 2026-10-28) ships with the 222-rule port, which is deferred pending the upstream fetch — not claimed here.
C-13.1.guard: test/secret-guard.test.mjs::a fiction token does not exempt a real secret beside it
